newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-LEHMAN LEADS FULKE BY TWO SHOTS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-LEHMAN LEADS FULKE BY TWO SHOTS.

text.p: Tom Lehman continued his superb buildup to next week's defence of his British Open title by holding off dogged Swede Pierre Fulke in the third round of the Loch Lomond World Invitational on Friday.
The rugged 38-year-old American took advantage of fine conditions to fire his third sub-par round, this one a four-under-par 67, and reach a 15-under total of 198 for a two- shot lead on Fulke.

The unheralded 26-year-old Swede followed the completion of his weather-delayed, seven-under-par second round 64 early on Friday with another excellent performance in the exalted company of Lehman and 1996 U.S. Open champion Steve Jones.
Though he bogeyed the last for the second time on the day, his composed 66 left him on 13 under par 200, two ahead of Jones who compiled a 68 to hold third place on 202.
One of his seven birdies came at the short eighth, where he has taken just five strokes in three rounds. He aced it on Wednesday.
U.S. Open champion Ernie Els was fourth after a 65 for 204. Greg Norman bogeyed the last to fall back into a share of fifth place with Englishman Paul Curry, the joint first round leader.
They shot 69 and 70 respectively for 205, eight under par.
There was a four-way tie for seventh between Swedes Joakim Haeggman, the other first round leader, and Mathias Gronberg, American Glen Day and Englishman Paul Broadhurst.
Play was again slow, Lehman's group taking five hours and five minutes.
Some players, particularly Colin Montgomerie but supported by Lehman, Ernie Els and Greg Norman, were criticial of officials for allowing it.

The other three said that on the U.S. Tour players were fined $1,000 without warning if they were slow or out of position and after a second fine were penalised a stroke and another $1,000 for a third offence.
"There probably hasn't been a penalty stroke this year because no-one likes getting fined $1,000 dollars," Lehman said.
Tournament referee Mike Stewart said he and his staff were doing the best they could to get the players round, "but it is not a race out there to get them round as quickly as possible."
He did not say if there had been any slow play warnings on Friday.
Lehman continued to be pleased with his play though he took his first bogey of the week at the fourth when he pulled his approach left.
It hit a spectator there which saved Lehman from a difficult lie on a rocky beach beside the shimmering Loch Lomond, but from the greenside rough he chipped awkwardly and two-putted.
Then he made five birdies, four in succession from the seventh with putts ranging from five to 30 feet.
Fulke, who has missed his last seven halfway cuts, was four under par when he resumed his second round on Friday after Thursday's delay caused by electrical storms.
Up at 0445 local (0345 GMT), he arrived at the course at 0530 (0430 GMT and it was some 13 hours later before he finished.
But after rounding off his 64 and tagging on a 66, he loved it. "It was a thrill to play as well as I did and to play with such great players as Tom and Syeve. They were great guys," he said.
He outscored them both, Lehman by a shot and Jones by two. "He putted very well and played smart," Lehman said.
Els played with Montgomerie, whom he has beaten head-to-head for both his U.S. Open victories, in 1994 and again last month.
Once again he held the upper hand, outscoring the Scot by five strokes, 65 to 70, though he refused to read any more into it than that.
Els, who took two weeks off after his U.S. Open triumph at Congressional, improved his score again after earlier rounds of 70 and 69.
"I'm quite satisfied but the weather is making it very playable with no wind and the fairways and greens holding," he said.
Montgomerie, who won the Irish Open with a spectacular closing 62 on Sunday, was not unhappy with his play in his 70.

"I think I am thinking about next week too much. I am not putting well and, yes, I think I have one eye on Troon," he said of next week's Open venue where his father is the club secretary and where there is already pressure on him to do well.
